emails.subject: You are not lazy
emails.preview: So why has the revenue stopped moving?
body: Let me start where the book starts.
You're no slacker. Nobody builds a six-figure company from nothing by being lazy.
Effort is the one thing you have never been short of.
Here's what I've watched for twenty years, first as an owner, then helping thousands of owners grow.
Talented people trip over the same invisible shoelaces. Every time.
Broken lead forms. Bad hires. No systems. Missed follow-ups.
Basic, fixable, unglamorous things.
And instead of stopping to tie the laces, they run harder. More hours. More hustle. Another marketing spend.
The ceiling arrives anyway, because the owner is the ceiling.
I'm going to be blunt with you, and I'll keep being blunt, because I respect anyone who has built something real.
What you have is a diagnosis problem.
You don't yet know which part of your business is weakest. So you keep improving the parts that already work.
That's where the effort keeps disappearing.
The Million-Dollar Scorecard exists for exactly this. Five sections. Score each statement one to five. Your lowest section is your primary constraint, and it goes first.
One rule travels with it, and it's the most important sentence in the book.
Do not work on scale while instability exists. Growth does not fix broken businesses. It exposes them.
Take the Scorecard before you read another chapter. Twenty-five statements, 10 to 15 minutes, and you'll know where to start.
[URL NEEDED: free 25-question Million-Dollar Scorecard in the reader portal]
Jim

emails.subject: Michael Gerber was right
emails.preview: The line that explains your entire calendar.
body: There's a line from Michael Gerber's The E-Myth that I've carried through four companies.
You're working in the business instead of on it.
Owners nod at that line and then go straight back to working in the business. So let me put a sharper point on it.
You may own the company. In practice, you are its hardest-working and best-compensated employee.
Here's the test. If you went dark for a week, what stops?
If the answer is quoting, or hiring, or the phone, or invoicing, then those jobs belong to you personally. You're the choke point on every one of them.
The cost of that goes beyond your calendar. If you do everything for your business, then you are the business. Nobody buys a business like that. You're locked in for life.
Now the useful part.
Most owners assume getting out from under this costs a fortune. It usually costs less than the company picnic.
Run the arithmetic from Chapter 5. Bringing a bookkeeper in-house costs you $35,000. Outsourcing the same role runs about $2,000 a month.
If the outsourced version does the work, why spend the $35,000?
Same story with HR. Same with legal. Same with the accounting you've been doing at 10pm on Sundays.
There's a side benefit nobody mentions. Listen to these two sentences.
"I'll find an attorney to look at that."
"I'll run that by my attorney."
Both are true. One of them sounds like a company.
Pick one job this week that only you do. Find out what handing it to a professional actually costs.
Jim

emails.subject: A question, no pitch
emails.preview: Something I've been wondering about you.
body: I play a lot of golf. More than seventy rounds a year, which is either a hobby or a diagnosis.
I love it because golf is played against yourself. On a par four with a wicked dogleg, the only thing standing between you and a birdie is you. Your swing, your focus, your read of the wind.
Small flaws get punished. Small gains get rewarded.
Business works the same way.
Here's the part I think about more than I'd like.
I've played plenty of rounds with owners who spent all eighteen holes on the phone. Technically on a golf course. Spiritually in a conference room.
Their playing partners know more about their Q3 revenue than their spouse does.
I've been that guy. I'm not judging him.
Anyway. I've been thinking about the people reading this book, and I want to ask you something.
If you vanished for one week with no phone, what would break first?
Be specific. Whatever came to mind in the first two seconds is usually the honest answer.
Just hit reply and tell me, {{contact.first_name}}. I read these myself.
Jim

emails.subject: Nice hustle, kid
emails.preview: What I learned lined up against a wall.
body: I was eleven the first time somebody paid me for a day's work.
Boston. Hyde Park. My parents signed me up for the city's caddy camp so I'd be outdoors for the summer.
A UPS truck collected us downtown and drove us out to one of the public courses. We got a couple of hours of training.
Then they lined us up against a wall.
We stood there while golfers looked us over and decided whether they wanted a child carrying their clubs that day. Less Caddyshack, more Lord of the Flies with golf bags.
If you got picked, you walked eighteen holes. Four hours in the sun.
At the end, the golfer paid you whatever loose change happened to be rattling around his pocket.
One time a guy shook my hand and said, "nice hustle, kid."
That was the entire payment. I couldn't even buy a Snickers with it.
I've thought about that wall for most of my life, because I spent a good stretch of my career standing against a different one.
I did the work. Somebody else decided what it was worth. My day got set by whoever called first.
That's the treadmill. It has nothing to do with how hard you're willing to work.
Eleven-year-olds work hard.
What got me off the wall was help. Honest, occasionally uncomfortable advice from people who had already done what I was trying to do.
That's the whole reason this book exists. I'd rather hand you that now than watch you spend another five years working it out alone.
Jim

emails.subject: What this morning looked like
emails.preview: A quiet hour, and a business that ran anyway.

I had coffee and read for an hour this morning. Nobody called. Nothing was on fire.
I want to tell you about the version of that morning I remember best, from the back half of Taradel.
We were generating around two hundred leads a day.
By eight in the morning those leads were getting answered, fast, by people who had been with us for years. Our average employee tenure was eight years. They knew the answer before I did.
Orders were going out. Campaigns were running. Staples and the USPS were sending small businesses our way while I sat in a kitchen in Richmond.
None of it needed me that morning.
The work still happened. It just stopped depending on me being awake for it.
Let me be careful here, because this is quieter than it sounds. There was no yacht. Nothing about that morning was exciting.
That's exactly what makes it worth having. An ordinary weekday where the business runs without you is the actual prize.
You still work. You get to choose what you work on.
Right now, other people choose for you.
That's the gap the next ninety days can close.
Jim

emails.subject: The dumbest guy in the room
emails.preview: What I found sitting with seven-figure founders.
body: <!-- SWAP WHEN AVAILABLE: replace with a real client case study once Jim has one -->
I spent years in a CEO roundtable.
Founders running multimillion-dollar companies. Real revenue, real teams, real payroll.
I walked into the first meeting braced to be the dumbest guy in the room.
Turns out we were all the dumbest guy in the room. Just about different things.
Broken lead forms. Bad hires. No systems. Missed opportunities.
That was the list. Every quarter, in a room full of people who had already cleared the hurdle.
One meeting has stayed with me.
A member named Michael was on the hot seat. Commodity services, brutal market, thousand-dollar jobs.
He had done the hard parts. Google presence dialed in. Sales team in place. Operations and delivery tight.
He asked the room what to do next, grinning.
We found it inside ten minutes. He was generating leads beautifully and answering them slowly.
So I read out the response-time numbers. Call a prospect back inside one minute and your odds of acquiring them go up 391 percent. After five minutes, sales take a nosedive.
Michael stopped grinning.
At the next roundtable he reported that his new speed-to-lead habit had made a significant difference.
That was the whole fix. Answering the phone faster.
Here's why I'm telling you this.
The things holding back seven-figure companies are boring, basic and fixable. Yours almost certainly are too.
That should land as relief.
Boring problems have known answers. You are not facing anything exotic.
Jim

emails.subject: One man to thirty million
emails.preview: What actually moved the number was unglamorous.
body: <!-- SWAP WHEN AVAILABLE: replace with a real client case study once Jim has one -->
Taradel started as one guy with a phone. That guy was me.
By the time I sold it we had 25,000 small business customers and thirty million in annual revenue. Inc. 5000 for twelve straight years.
People assume there was a moment. A big idea, a lucky break.
We had some good breaks. What moved the number was a stack of unglamorous systems, built one at a time.
Let me show you one, because owners get this one wrong more than any other.
Hiring.
For years I hired the way most owners do. Check the qualifications, have a conversation, trust your gut, done by Friday.
That's how I ended up with people who cost me money and cost me mornings.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics puts a bad hire at 30 percent of their first-year wages, minimum. My experience says that number is generous.
Then we built a process. Three interviews.
First the manager who would supervise them. Then three or four of our best performers who would work alongside them. Then me.
Everyone had to say yes. Anyone could veto for any reason, including a reason they couldn't put into words.
Our average employee tenure reached eight years.
Almost every hiring mistake we made after that came from overriding our own process.
That process is written down now. So is the pipeline system, the retention math, the checklists behind all of it.

They sit inside the Million-Dollar Hurdle Training Kit. Five playbooks, five AI training files that teach ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini to run these systems in your business, and a ninety-day plan keyed to your Scorecard.
$67. In your inbox in about two minutes. Thirty days to get every penny back.

emails.subject: Yes, I sell AI files
emails.preview: So here is exactly what I think of AI.
body: Let me get in front of something.
Part of what I sell trains an AI to run my systems inside your business.
You may have read that and thought: wonderful, another guy promising a robot will fix my company.
Fair enough. Here's my honest position.
I co-founded a company called Paycile. We put AI into payments, reconciliation and cash flow forecasting. I use this stuff every day and I've watched where it earns its keep.
AI is very good at work you have already defined.
Hand it three years of customer data and ask what your best customers have in common. It will find things you missed.
Hand it your callback script and it will run it at two in the morning without complaining once.
Here's the part that gets skipped in the demos.
It has no idea what your business stands for.
I wrote in the book that you can't ask ChatGPT for a set of core values, print them out and call the job done. Those come from you.
Same with who you promote. Same with who you fire. Same with the customer you turn away because the money isn't worth the drama.
Think of it as a caddy. It reads the yardage, hands you the club, carries the bag.
You still have to swing.
That's why the playbooks come before the training files. You learn the system, then you teach it to the machine.
An untrained AI inside an undefined business just makes poor decisions faster.
Jim

emails.subject: More leads will not save you
emails.preview: The arithmetic on customers you already lost.
body: Every owner I have ever met reaches for the same lever.
More leads. More ads. Another salesperson. More revenue solves everything.
I reached for it too. It's the obvious move and it feels like progress.
Then I ran the arithmetic in Chapter 7, and it changed how I think.
Say you pay $100 to acquire a customer, and nine out of ten never come back.
To hold a hundred paying customers on your books, you have to buy nine hundred new ones every year.
That's $90,000 a year to stand still.
Now cut that churn in half. Same pricing, same product, same marketing spend.
You save $40,000 a year.
That money was already yours. You were spending it to replace people who had chosen you once already.
Pour more leads into that business and you get a bigger version of the same leak.
W. E. Deming made the point long before I did. Growing the wrong way hurts more than it helps.
Which brings me back to the one rule from the book.
Do not work on scale while instability exists. Growth does not fix broken businesses. It exposes them.
So before you spend another dollar on lead generation, go and score yourself.
Five sections, twenty-five statements, about 10 to 15 minutes.
Your lowest section is where the money is leaking out.

The work happens because a system runs it. Your people know the answer before you do.
You still work. You get to choose what you work on.
Most owners reading this are in one. A decent number are in two. Almost nobody arrives at three by accident.

emails.subject: Three things you're telling yourself
emails.preview: I have heard all three. Here is my answer.
body: I've been having a version of this conversation for twenty years.
Same three objections, in roughly the same order, every time.
Let me take them one at a time.
"I'm already overwhelmed. This is one more thing to learn."
This is the one I hear most, and I understand it. Your week is full. It has been full for years.
Here's what I'd say back.
You're overwhelmed because you're spending every waking minute on the wrong stuff.
Quoting jobs a trained estimator could quote. Answering questions your team should be able to answer. Fixing problems that a written process would have prevented on Tuesday.
This is the right work. It's the work that empties out the rest of the week.
Ninety days of it buys back hours you're currently donating to your own business.
"Jim, I'm broke."
I've heard that one from a man walking back to a brand new Land Rover.
No cash to spare, and a new deck on the house. Not a single cent going spare, and a $57 steak on Friday night.
I say this with affection. Sir, your watch costs more than my first car.
Real cash constraints exist and I take them seriously. Some months payroll is a genuine decision. If that's you, work the book on your own and keep your money.
For everyone else, run the comparison.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics puts one bad hire at 30 percent of their first-year wages, minimum. On a $60,000 role that's $18,000 gone, and almost nobody makes that mistake only once.
The kit costs $67. Set the two numbers side by side and decide.
"My problems are more complicated."
Everybody says this. Almost nobody is right.
I've sat with hundreds of owners who were certain their situation was exotic. Then we'd go looking.
Broken lead form. Hiring on gut feel. Nobody following up after the quote goes out. Same short list, in company after company.
That should land as good news. Complicated problems need a genius. Basic problems need a process.

emails.subject: The $2,500 mistake
emails.preview: How I knew who should replace me.
body: Wendy made a mistake that cost Taradel $2,500.
I was about to speak at the National Postal Forum. She realized the error and came to me, horrified.
By then we were doing eight figures a year. $2,500 was a rounding error.
That's how I saw it. Wendy tore herself apart over it.
Which is the exact moment I became certain she should replace me.
After the event I told her so. "Wendy, I want one direct report, and it's you. Maybe that's extreme, but that's how much I trust you."
She became president of Taradel after I left.
Here's why I'm telling you.
Most owners quietly aim to be indispensable. Everything routes through them and they wear it like a badge.
I understand the instinct. Your business is your child and you're determined to solo parent, even if it kills you.
Now think about the day you want out.
If you do everything for your business, then you are the business. Nobody buys that. You'd be selling a job with your name on it.
The owner who makes himself replaceable ends up holding something else entirely. A company that runs on people and systems.
That company has a price. Somebody can write you a check for it.
Making yourself replaceable is chapter 15, and it's most of the point of the whole book.
One of the five playbooks in the Training Kit is called The Replaceable Owner.
It's the one owners are most nervous to open.

emails.subject: Two ways to spend a year
emails.preview: Both take twelve months. One arrives somewhere.
body: There are two ways to spend the next twelve months.
Path one. Everything stays the way it is.
You keep quoting the big jobs personally. You keep hiring on gut feel and hoping it works out. The phone keeps setting your agenda before you've finished your coffee.
Revenue moves a little. Some months are good ones. The shape of the week never changes.
Next July you're still in the work, twelve months older, running the same day.
And here's the part nobody says out loud.
If you do everything for your business, then you are the business. No one is going to buy that business from you when you want to leave.
You're locked in for life.
Path two. You pick one section and work it for ninety days.
Just one. Your lowest one.
Ninety days later that section runs on a documented system instead of running on you. Then you take the next lowest.
Four quarters. Four sections. The same twelve months either way.
Next July you're on the system. Your people know the answer before you do. A week away costs you nothing.
Both paths cost you something. Path one costs you the year and hands you the same business back. Path two costs you focused attention on unglamorous work you've been avoiding.
I'm not asking you to choose today.
Just notice that you're standing at a fork, and that standing still quietly picks path one for you.
Jim

emails.subject: A little company out of Richmond
emails.preview: The call I took in an Uber.
body: In 2015 we got a call at Taradel. Staples wanted to talk.
Yes, that Staples. The Easy Button people.
Their CEO wanted to grow past office supplies by partnering with companies who could do more for their customers. They'd bring the customers. We'd bring the direct mail platform.
We pitched hard. We agreed to white label our service under their brand and gave them a revenue share.
Two weeks later I was in the back of an Uber heading to the airport when my phone rang.
"We're in."
Landing it was the fun part. Executing it was the work.
We had to train hundreds of Staples sales reps across the country on the nuances of direct mail targeting. If you've never tried that, I envy you.
When the dust settled, it had become the most successful launch ever for their print division. For us it meant millions in revenue under their name.
Not bad for a little company out of Richmond.
Later the USPS put a direct link from their own website to a platform we built for them.
I want to be careful about the lesson here, because it has very little to do with luck.
Staples called a company. By then Taradel looked like one from the outside and ran like one on the inside.
Big partners want the same things your best customers want. Somebody answers fast. Somebody keeps the promise. The place works whether the founder is on a plane that day.
You build that reputation in ordinary weeks, long before anyone important notices.
I had a phrase for the owners we served back then. They're small businesses, but they're real.
Twelve straight years on the Inc. 5000 came from that same unglamorous work. Answering fast. Hiring slowly. Keeping good people eight years.
Somebody eventually says the same about your company. That's the quiet outcome underneath all of this.
Jim
